OXON HILL, Maryland (CNN) -- Crew members of the Maersk Alabama, safely returned to the United States after being attacked by pirates last week off the coast of Somalia, recounted their harrowing ordeal on Thursday. Navy personnel recovered the lifeboat from which Maersk Alabama Captain Richard Phillips was rescued on Sunday.

"They start firing before they climb, with AK-47," crew member Zahid Reza recalled. "I was scared for my life. I was almost close to that. And they tried to shoot me many times," he said, gesturing toward his head. "Pointing gun all over. Here, there, in the back."

The pirates attempted to board the U.S.-flagged cargo ship three times before succeeding on their fourth attempt, fellow crew member William Rios reported. He added that although the groups of pirates were distinct, he believes they were working in coordination. Rios said he had been working on deck when he was summoned back to help lock down the ship. Then, he recounted, gunshots rang out, and an alarm sounded to alert all crew members to wake up and report to the deck.

"We went to our training," he said, though he declined to elaborate: "If I tell you all what we did, pirates, they would know."

According to Reza, the pirates intended to demand a $3 million ransom. He explained that he and the ship's chief engineer managed to take one of the pirates hostage. Reza said he had persuaded the pirate -- whom he described as a young man, perhaps 18 or 19 -- to trust him, emphasizing their shared faith despite the fact that he is Bangladeshi and the pirate was Somali.

"His name is Abdul," Reza said. "I told him, 'Trust me. I am Muslim; you are Muslim.'"

He told Abdul that he would take him to the engine room to find additional crew members. When they arrived, the room was dark, he recalled, and he was unaware that the ship's chief engineer was inside. According to Reza, the chief engineer lunged at the pirate first, after which Reza stabbed him with his knife, and together the two men bound the pirate's hands and feet. Reza admitted that he had intended to kill the young man, but the chief engineer told him, "No, we need him alive."

"He was fighting me and chief engineer, to get away from us. A lot of yelling, shouting and screaming."

Rios said he then went to the lifeboat, where Captain Richard Phillips was being held, in an attempt to exchange Abdul for Phillips, but the effort was unsuccessful. The captain -- who had offered himself as a hostage in exchange for the freedom of his crew -- was rescued by U.S. Navy SEALs on Sunday. Operating from the nearby guided-missile destroyer USS Bainbridge, the SEALs fatally shot three pirates and freed Phillips. A fourth pirate was taken into custody.

"I feel great they got killed," Reza said. "I am happy." He added that he was proud of the Navy.

Phillips arrived in Mombasa, Kenya, aboard the Bainbridge on Thursday. The crew, meanwhile, arrived at Andrews Air Force Base in Maryland overnight.

Rios praised Phillips as "outstanding; he's extraordinary; he's [a] very brave man." Another crew member, John White, said they were "damn lucky to be alive."

Rios called for enhanced security in the Gulf of Aden. "Put more military to patrol the waterway for us transporting material back and forth," he urged. "... All the countries got to get involved with this."

Reza echoed the appeal. "I think government should get involved," he said. "They should think about our safety, yes. ... This piracy is getting bigger and bigger."

CNN's Paul Courson, Virginia Nicolaidis and Dugald McConnell contributed to this report.

Navy forces had retrieved the lifeboat where Captain Richard Phillips had been held captive until his Sunday rescue.

"They start firing before they climb, with AK-47," said crew member Zahid Reza. Fearing for his life, he recalled how close he came to death. "And they tried to shoot me many times," he added, gesturing toward his head. "Pointing gun all over. Here, there, in the back."

According to another sailor, William Rios, the pirates made three failed attempts to climb aboard the American-flagged cargo vessel before finally succeeding on their fourth try. He noted that while the attacking groups were distinct, he believed they were coordinating their efforts. Rios explained that he had been on deck when he received orders to return and secure the ship. Shortly after, gunfire erupted and an alarm sounded, signaling everyone to wake up and report to the deck.

"We went to our training," Rios said, though he wouldn't elaborate: "If I tell you all what we did, pirates, they would know."

Reza revealed that the attackers planned to demand $3 million in ransom. He recounted how he and the vessel's chief engineer managed to seize one of the pirates and hold him captive. Reza said he won over the pirate—a youth he estimated to be around 18 or 19—by emphasizing their shared faith, noting that he himself is from Bangladesh while the pirate was Somali.

"His name is Abdul," Reza said. "I told him, 'Trust me. I am Muslim; you are Muslim.'"

He said he convinced Abdul to accompany him to the engine room under the pretext of locating additional crew members. Once there, the space was pitch dark, and Reza was unaware that the chief engineer was already present. According to Reza, the chief engineer lunged at the pirate first, after which Reza stabbed the young man with his knife, and together they bound his hands and feet.

Reza admitted he wanted to kill the teenager, but the chief engineer stopped him, insisting, "No, we need him alive."

"He was fighting me and chief engineer, to get away from us. A lot of yelling, shouting and screaming."

Rios said he attempted to trade Abdul for Captain Phillips at the lifeboat where the captain was being detained, but the exchange failed. Phillips, who had volunteered himself as a hostage so his crew could go free, was ultimately rescued Sunday by U.S. Navy SEALs. Operating from the USS Bainbridge, a guided-missile destroyer positioned nearby, the SEALs killed three pirates and freed the captain. The fourth pirate was taken into custody.

"I feel great they got killed," Reza remarked. "I am happy." He expressed his pride in the Navy.

Phillips reached Mombasa, Kenya, aboard the Bainbridge on Thursday, while the crew touched down overnight at Andrews Air Force Base in Maryland.

Rios praised the captain, describing him as "outstanding; he's extraordinary; he's [a] very brave man." Crew member John White reflected that they were "damn lucky to be alive."

Rios urged for stronger protection in the Gulf of Aden. "Put more military to patrol the waterway for us transporting material back and forth," he said. "... All the countries got to get involved with this."

Reza voiced the same concern. "I think government should get involved," he stated. "They should think about our safety, yes. ... This piracy is getting bigger and bigger."

CNN's Paul Courson, Virginia Nicolaidis and Dugald McConnell contributed to this report.

# Crew Members Recount Harrowing 2009 Maersk Alabama Hijacking

## Firsthand Accounts Emerge from Historic Pirate Standoff

The 2009 hijacking of the U.S.-flagged cargo ship Maersk Alabama by Somali pirates became one of the most dramatic maritime crises in recent memory, culminating in a military rescue operation that captivated the world. In the aftermath, crew members shared their experiences of the four-day ordeal.

---

## The Attack Begins

On April 8, 2009, the Maersk Alabama was navigating waters approximately 240 nautical miles off the Somali coast, en route to Mombasa, Kenya, carrying food aid and other cargo. The 17,000-ton container ship carried a crew of 20 unarmed American sailors.

Crew members described spotting the pirates approaching in a small skiff during the early morning hours. Four armed Somali men managed to board the vessel despite evasive maneuvers by the crew.

According to accounts from crew members, the sailors had prepared for such a possibility. Chief Engineer Mike Perry and others activated defensive protocols, with much of the crew retreating to a secured "safe room" in the engine room area.

---

## Crew Resistance and Countermeasures

In interviews following their return, crew members detailed how they fought back against the heavily armed intruders:

- **Disabling the ship:** The crew reportedly cut electrical power to disorient the pirates and slow the ship.
- **Hiding in the engine room:** Much of the crew sheltered in a sweltering, darkened safe room, communicating and coordinating resistance efforts.
- **Capturing a pirate:** Crew members managed to overpower and briefly detain one of the pirates, the group's leader, whom they hoped to use in a prisoner exchange.

The crew described conditions as tense and physically grueling, enduring extreme heat in their hiding spot for extended hours while uncertain of their fate.

---

## Captain Phillips Taken Hostage

The situation shifted when the planned exchange broke down. Captain Richard Phillips was taken by the pirates as they attempted to leave the ship. Crew accounts and later reporting indicated that Phillips offered himself to protect his crew, though some details of these events have been the subject of differing accounts and subsequent legal disputes.

The four pirates, along with Captain Phillips as their hostage, boarded one of the ship's enclosed lifeboats and set out toward the Somali coast.

---

## The Standoff at Sea

The U.S. Navy responded rapidly, dispatching the destroyer USS Bainbridge to the scene, later joined by additional vessels including the USS Halyburton. The FBI became involved in hostage negotiations.

For several days, the drifting lifeboat became the center of an international standoff. Captain Phillips remained captive in cramped, dangerous conditions. At one point, he reportedly attempted to escape by jumping into the water, but was recaptured by his captors.

Negotiators worked to secure Phillips' release while Navy SEAL teams were positioned for a potential rescue operation.

---

## The Dramatic Rescue

On April 12, 2009—Easter Sunday—the standoff reached its climax. With Captain Phillips' life judged to be in imminent danger, Navy SEAL snipers positioned aboard the USS Bainbridge took action.

In a coordinated operation authorized under presidential rules of engagement, three SEAL marksmen simultaneously shot and killed three of the pirates. The fourth pirate, the leader who had been aboard the Bainbridge during negotiations, was taken into custody.

Captain Phillips was rescued unharmed and transferred to safety aboard the USS Bainbridge.

---

## Aftermath

**Captain Phillips** was hailed as a hero for his role in the crisis. He later authored a memoir, "A Captain's Duty," which became the basis for the 2013 film "Captain Phillips" starring Tom Hanks.

**The surviving pirate,** Abduwali Muse, was brought to the United States, tried in federal court, and sentenced to more than 33 years in prison.

**The crew** returned home to reunions with family. However, some crew members later filed lawsuits alleging that the shipping company and Maersk Line had knowingly sent them into dangerous waters. Certain crew members also publicly disputed aspects of the popular narrative surrounding Captain Phillips' decisions, offering alternative accounts of the events leading to the hijacking.

---

## A Historic Maritime Event

The Maersk Alabama hijacking marked the first successful pirate seizure of a U.S.-flagged vessel in roughly two centuries. The incident drew international attention to the growing problem of Somali piracy and influenced subsequent maritime security policies, including expanded use of armed security personnel aboard commercial vessels.

The crew's collective actions during the crisis—and the precision of the military rescue—remain a defining chapter in modern maritime history.

---

*Note: This report synthesizes publicly reported accounts of the 2009 events. Some specific details of crew members' individual experiences have been the subject of varying accounts and legal proceedings.*

The confrontation reached its most perilous point when Captain Phillips was taken hostage aboard an enclosed lifeboat, setting off a days-long standoff at sea.

## The Ransom Demand

According to accounts from the crew, the pirates sought a substantial ransom in exchange for the captain and the vessel. The demand underscored the commercial motivations behind the surge in piracy that has plagued the region, where hijackings have become a lucrative enterprise for armed groups operating from the Somali coastline.

The standoff ultimately ended when Navy snipers, acting on authorization to use force amid concerns for the captain's safety, brought the hostage crisis to a close and freed Phillips.

## Calls for Greater Security

With the ordeal behind them, crew members used their homecoming to press for a stronger military response to piracy in the Gulf of Aden and surrounding waters. Several called for expanded naval protection for commercial shipping traveling through the dangerous corridor, one of the world's busiest maritime routes.

Crew members argued that merchant vessels remain vulnerable to attack and that a more robust and coordinated international military presence is needed to deter pirates and safeguard sailors. Their appeals echoed growing concerns within the shipping industry about the risks facing crews who transit the region.

The incident has intensified debate over how best to combat piracy off the Somali coast, including questions about arming merchant ships, coordinating international naval patrols, and addressing the instability on land that has fueled the rise in attacks.

For the crew of the Maersk Alabama, however, the immediate focus was reunion with loved ones — and gratitude for a safe return home following an ordeal few could have imagined.

# American Crew Recounts Dramatic Battle with Somali Pirates, Captain's Rescue

**Crew members of the U.S.-flagged cargo ship describe hand-to-hand fighting, a captured pirate, and the tense standoff that ended with their captain's rescue.**

Crew members of a U.S. cargo vessel returned home this week with harrowing accounts of how they fought off a band of Somali pirates who boarded their ship, managing to overpower and capture one of the attackers before their captain was taken hostage and later rescued.

The confrontation began when the pirates approached the ship in a small skiff and scaled the hull, catching the mostly unarmed merchant crew by surprise. What followed, sailors said, was a chaotic struggle across the decks and passageways of the vessel.

Zahid Reza, a crew member who was among those who confronted the intruders, described tackling one of the pirates during the melee.

"I saw him and I just grabbed him," Reza said. "We took him down. I had him and we tied him up. He was young, just a kid really, but he had a gun."

Reza said the crew held the captured pirate for hours, hoping to use him as leverage in negotiations to secure the release of others being held.

William Rios, another member of the crew, recalled the fear that gripped the men as they hid in the darkened engine room and other compartments, listening for the footsteps of the armed pirates searching for them.

"We were quiet, we shut everything down," Rios said. "You could hear them walking around, looking for us. Nobody knew what was going to happen. We just kept thinking about the captain."

The crew's captain had offered himself to the pirates in an effort to protect his men, sailors said—a decision that left him in the hands of the attackers as they eventually departed the ship. The standoff shifted to a small lifeboat, where the captain was held at gunpoint.

"He did it for us," Rios said of the captain. "He gave himself up so the rest of us would be safe. That's the kind of man he is."

The ordeal ended when U.S. naval forces, which had rushed to the scene, executed a rescue operation that freed the captain unharmed. Crew members said they erupted in relief when word reached them that their captain was safe.

"When we heard he was okay, everybody was just—there are no words," Reza said. "We were praying the whole time."

The sailors credited their training, their teamwork, and their captain's leadership with getting them through the crisis. Several said they were grateful to the military personnel who came to their aid.

"These guys, the Navy, they saved his life," Rios said. "We owe them everything."

As they reunited with families, the crew reflected on how close the situation had come to tragedy—and on the bond forged among men who had faced danger together on the open sea.

"You never think it's going to happen to you," Reza said. "But when it does, you find out what people are made of."
